claim: AIM2 autoantibodies were detected in 41/131 (31.3%) SLE patients and 2/49 (4.1%) controls.
source: 41/131 (31.3%) of SLE versus 2/49 (4.1%) of healthy controls were anti-AIM2-positive (P < 0.001) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunoprecipitation assays measuring AIM2 autoantibodies in patient and control sera, with results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Anti-AIM2 antibodies are significantly more prevalent in SLE patients compared to healthy controls (P < 0.001).
source: 41/131 (31.3%) of SLE versus 2/49 (4.1%) of healthy controls were anti-AIM2-positive (P < 0.001) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Statistical significance (P < 0.001) is provided from comparison of AIM2 antibody prevalence between SLE patients and controls.

claim: Anti-AIM2 antibodies are strongly associated with anti-IFI16 antibodies in SLE patients.
source: Interestingly, anti-AIM2 antibodies were strongly associated with both anti-IFI16 and anti-DNA antibodies in the SLE samples measured on the day of visit (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: The association is demonstrated through data analysis of SLE patient samples, shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Anti-AIM2 antibodies are strongly associated with anti-DNA antibodies in SLE patients.
source: Interestingly, anti-AIM2 antibodies were strongly associated with both anti-IFI16 and anti-DNA antibodies in the SLE samples measured on the day of visit (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: The association is demonstrated through data analysis of SLE patient samples, shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Anti-AIM2 antibodies are associated with higher SLEDAI scores in SLE patients (2.29 ± 2.3 vs 1.05 ± 1.61, P = 0.0026).
source: We found that anti-AIM2 antibodies were associated with higher measures of SLEDAI (2.29 ± 2.3 vs 1.05 ± 1.61, P = 0.0026, Table 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of SLEDAI scores comparing anti-AIM2 positive and negative patients, with data presented in Table 1.

claim: The association between anti-AIM2 antibodies and higher SLEDAI scores is largely driven by the immunology component.
source: We found that anti-AIM2 antibodies were associated with higher measures of SLEDAI (2.29 ± 2.3 vs 1.05 ± 1.61, P = 0.0026, Table 1), which was largely driven by the immunology component.
evidence: This is an inference based on analysis of SLEDAI component scores in the patient cohort.

claim: Anti-AIM2 antibodies are associated with skin domain disease activity in SLE patients (26.8% vs 12.2%, P = 0.0463).
source: Anti-AIM2 antibodies were associated with the presence of disease activity in the skin domain of the SLEDAI index at the date of blood draw: 11/41 (26.8%) of anti-AIM2 positive patients had scores > 0 in this domain, compared to 11/90 (12.2%) of anti-AIM2 negative patients (P = 0.0463).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of skin domain SLEDAI scores comparing anti-AIM2 positive and negative patients.

claim: Anti-AIM2 antibodies are associated with increased SLE Physician Global Disease Activity scores (0.63 ± 0.55 vs 0.43 ± 0.51, P = 0.0333).
source: Anti-AIM2 antibodies were also associated with a small but significant increase (0.63 ± 0.55 vs 0.43 ± 0.51, P = 0.0333) in the SLE Physician Global Disease Activity score, which is based solely on clinical estimation of SLE activity, rather than serologic indices.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Physician Global Disease Activity scores comparing anti-AIM2 positive and negative patients.

claim: Anti-AIM2 antibodies are significantly associated with anti-IFI16 antibodies with an odds ratio of 3.7 (P = 0.007, 95% CI 1.44–9.7) after multivariable analysis.
source: A multivariable analysis correcting for SLEDAI, anti-dsDNA, and C4 results demonstrated that anti-AIM2 antibodies were significantly associated with anti-IFI16 antibodies with an OR of 3.7 (P = 0.007, 95% CI 1.44–9.7).
evidence: The claim is supported by multivariable logistic regression analysis controlling for confounding variables.

claim: A subset of SLE patients (n = 9) with particularly high levels of anti-AIM2 antibodies (normalized OD >20) had higher SLEDAI values than both lower level anti-AIM2-positive and anti-AIM2-negative patients.
source: A subset of SLE patients (n = 9) demonstrated particularly high levels of anti-AIM2 antibodies with normalized OD >20 (Figure 1A). These patients had higher SLEDAI values than both lower level anti-AIM2-positive and anti-AIM2-negative patients (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of SLEDAI scores in patients stratified by anti-AIM2 antibody levels, with data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Among anti-AIM2 positive SLE patients, there is a higher prevalence of anti-Ro antibodies (44% vs 21%, P = 0.0114).
source: Among all anti-AIM2 positive patients, we found a higher prevalence of positivity for anti–Ro (18/41, 44% vs 19/90, 21%, P = 0.0114) and anti–La (10/41, 24% vs 7/90, 8%, P = 0.0125) antibodies (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of anti-Ro antibody prevalence comparing anti-AIM2 positive and negative patients, with data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Among anti-AIM2 positive SLE patients, there is a higher prevalence of anti-La antibodies (24% vs 8%, P = 0.0125).
source: Among all anti-AIM2 positive patients, we found a higher prevalence of positivity for anti–Ro (18/41, 44% vs 19/90, 21%, P = 0.0114) and anti–La (10/41, 24% vs 7/90, 8%, P = 0.0125) antibodies (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of anti-La antibody prevalence comparing anti-AIM2 positive and negative patients, with data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: SLE sera retain the ability to bind AIM2 following DNase treatment.
source: To address this, we pre-treated anti-AIM2 +SLE sera and the AIM2 IVTT product with DNase prior to combining them in the IP reaction, and found that SLE sera retained the ability to bind AIM2 following DNase treatment (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunoprecipitation assays performed with DNase-treated samples, shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: 8/10 anti-AIM2 positive SLE sera immunoprecipitated the isolated AIM2 PYRIN domain lacking the DNA-binding HIN domain.
source: To further confirm this, we also performed immunoprecipitation of AIM2 PYRIN domain (PYD) that lacks the DNA-binding HIN domain, finding that 8/10 anti-AIM2 +SLE sera immunoprecipitated the isolated AIM2 PYD in this assay.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunoprecipitation assays using AIM2 PYD construct.

claim: DNA is not required for AIM2 antibody binding in the immunoprecipitation assays.
source: Thus, DNA was not required for AIM2 binding in the samples assessed in these assays, confirming that this is a bona fide antibody specificity.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the DNase treatment and PYD domain experiments demonstrating antibody binding in the absence of DNA.

claim: There is no difference in anti-MNDA reactivity between healthy control and SLE sera (median AU HC = 1.279, median AU SLE = 1.228, P = 0.9319).
source: Despite the fact that antibodies against peptides derived from MNDA had been reported in some patients with SLE and other rheumatic diseases (van Beers et al., 2013), we did not identify any difference in anti-MNDA reactivity between healthy control and SLE sera (median AU HC = 1.279, median AU SLE = 1.228, P = 0.9319) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data comparing anti-MNDA antibody levels between healthy controls and SLE patients, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Antibodies against peptides derived from MNDA had been reported in some patients with SLE and other rheumatic diseases.
source: Despite the fact that antibodies against peptides derived from MNDA had been reported in some patients with SLE and other rheumatic diseases (van Beers et al., 2013), we did not identify any difference in anti-MNDA reactivity between healthy control and SLE sera (median AU HC = 1.279, median AU SLE = 1.228, P = 0.9319) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work (van Beers et al., 2013).

claim: 46/133 (34.6%) of Sjögren's Syndrome sera were positive for anti-AIM2 antibodies.
source: We therefore analyzed SS sera for the presence of anti-AIM2 antibodiesand found that 46/133 (34.6%) of SS sera were positive.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunoprecipitation assays measuring AIM2 autoantibodies in SS patient sera.

claim: In Sjögren's Syndrome, anti-IFI16 is not enriched in patients with anti-AIM2 antibodies (35% vs 28%, P = 0.4324).
source: In contrast to SLE, anti-IFI16 was not enriched in patients with anti-AIM2 antibodies in SS (35% anti-AIM2-positive and anti-IFI16-positive versus 28% anti-AIM2-negative and anti-IFI16-positive in SS, P = 0.4324)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing anti-IFI16 prevalence in anti-AIM2 positive versus negative SS patients.

claim: The association between anti-IFI16 and anti-AIM2 antibodies is specific to SLE.
source: In contrast to SLE, anti-IFI16 was not enriched in patients with anti-AIM2 antibodies in SS (35% anti-AIM2-positive and anti-IFI16-positive versus 28% anti-AIM2-negative and anti-IFI16-positive in SS, P = 0.4324), showing that the association between anti-IFI16 and anti-AIM2 antibodies is specific to SLE, where these immune responses are also associated with anti-dsDNA antibodies.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from comparing the association patterns between SLE and SS patient cohorts.

claim: Both IFI16 and AIM2 bind readily to neutrophil extracellular traps.
source: To test this hypothesis, we used NETs as a DNA substrate for ALR binding: neutrophils were stimulated to undergo NETosis with PMA, and then incubated with fluorescently labeled IFI16 and AIM2 proteins. We found that both ALRs bind readily to NETs (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence microscopy showing ALR binding to NETs, shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Co-localization of AIM2 and IFI16 along NET chromatin fibers is visible by confocal microscopy.
source: Co-localization of AIM2 and IFI16 along NET chromatin fibers was visible by confocal microscopy in this analysis, suggesting that both ALRs assemble into filaments on NET DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy imaging data showing co-localization of AIM2 and IFI16 on NETs.

claim: Both AIM2 and IFI16 assemble into filaments on NET DNA.
source: Co-localization of AIM2 and IFI16 along NET chromatin fibers was visible by confocal microscopy in this analysis, suggesting that both ALRs assemble into filaments on NET DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization pattern observed in confocal microscopy images.

claim: ALR-bound NETs show incomplete degradation by DNase I, with IFI16 and AIM2 remaining present and co-localized with MPO in some areas.
source: When NETs were first incubated with ALRs, however, we observed incomplete ALR-NET degradation by DNase I – in some areas, IFI16 and AIM2 remained present and co-localized with MPO (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing persistent ALR-NET structures after DNase treatment, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Observable DNA remains in areas of persistent ALR structures after DNase treatment, implying that ALRs partially shield NET DNA from degradation.
source: In addition, there was observable DNA remaining in these areas of persistent ALR structures, implying that the ALRs had partially shielded NET DNA from degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from microscopy observations showing DNA signal persisting in areas with ALR structures after DNase treatment.

claim: Both the protein and DNA components of the ALR-NET structure are resistant to DNase-mediated clearance.
source: This finding suggested that both the protein and DNA components of the ALR-NET structure are resistant to DNase-mediated clearance.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that both ALR proteins and DNA persist after DNase treatment.

claim: ALR-bound NETs are resistant to DNase I, leaving more DNA present following nuclease treatment.
source: To better quantify this, we employed a plate-based Sytox Green assay to measure the dsDNA content of NETs following exposure to DNase I (Figure 2E). This assay confirmed that ALR-bound NETs are resistant to DNase I, leaving more DNA present following nuclease treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative fluorimetry data measuring DNA content after DNase treatment, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ALRs bind to NETs, generating a protein-DNA structure with enhanced resistance to DNase-mediated clearance.
source: Together these experiments demonstrate that ALRs bind to NETs, generating a protein-DNA structure with enhanced resistance to DNase-mediated clearance.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of microscopy and quantitative assays showing ALR binding and DNase resistance.

claim: IFI16 blocks dsDNA degradation by DNase I in a fluorescence anisotropy assay.
source: To test the specificity of this observation, we utilized a fluorescence anisotropy assay to compare IFI16 against the catalytic domain of cGAS (cGAS-CD), to determine whether the property of DNA binding alone confers proteins with the ability to shield bound dsDNA from DNAse I (Figure 2F). In this second assay, we again observed that IFI16 blocked dsDNA degradation, while cGAS-CD did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data comparing IFI16 and cGAS-CD effects on DNA degradation, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: cGAS-CD does not block dsDNA degradation by DNase I in a fluorescence anisotropy assay.
source: To test the specificity of this observation, we utilized a fluorescence anisotropy assay to compare IFI16 against the catalytic domain of cGAS (cGAS-CD), to determine whether the property of DNA binding alone confers proteins with the ability to shield bound dsDNA from DNAse I (Figure 2F). In this second assay, we again observed that IFI16 blocked dsDNA degradation, while cGAS-CD did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data comparing IFI16 and cGAS-CD effects on DNA degradation, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The ability to shield dsDNA from nuclease does not appear to be a universal property of all DNA-binding proteins.
source: Thus, the ability to shield dsDNA from nuclease does not appear to be a universal property of all DNA-binding proteins, and other factors (such as the ability to oligomerize) may be required for this behavior.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential behavior of IFI16 versus cGAS-CD in the DNase protection assay.

claim: Other factors such as the ability to oligomerize may be required for proteins to shield dsDNA from nuclease.
source: Thus, the ability to shield dsDNA from nuclease does not appear to be a universal property of all DNA-binding proteins, and other factors (such as the ability to oligomerize) may be required for this behavior.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known oligomerization properties of IFI16 and the observed differences between IFI16 and cGAS-CD.

claim: AIM2 is highly expressed in MPO-positive infiltrating cells in lupus nephritis biopsies.
source: We found that AIM2 was highly expressed in MPO-positive infiltrating cells (Figure 3A), while IFI16 was expressed more broadly throughout renal cell types (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data from lupus nephritis tissue sections, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IFI16 is expressed more broadly throughout renal cell types in lupus nephritis biopsies.
source: We found that AIM2 was highly expressed in MPO-positive infiltrating cells (Figure 3A), while IFI16 was expressed more broadly throughout renal cell types (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data from lupus nephritis tissue sections, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NETs containing both AIM2 and IFI16 are detected in glomerular and interstitial infiltrates in lupus nephritis.
source: We detected NETs containing both AIM2 and IFI16 in glomerular and interstitial infiltrates (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data from lupus nephritis tissue sections, shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: High magnification z-stack imaging confirms that ALR-containing structures in lupus nephritis represent extracellular DNA that co-stains for MPO and AIM2 or IFI16, consistent with ALR-bound NETs.
source: High magnification, z-stack imaging (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) confirmed that these structures represented extracellular DNA that co-stained for MPO and AIM2 or IFI16, consistent with ALR-bound NETs, rather than adjacent or overlapping cell nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by z-stack confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: AIM2 and IFI16 bind NETs in the setting of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis.
source: In summary, our immunostaining experiments provide evidence that AIM2 and IFI16 bind NETs in the setting of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, establishing AIM2 and IFI16 as NET-bound SLE autoantigens.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the immunofluorescence microscopy data showing ALR-NET co-localization in lupus nephritis tissues.

claim: AIM2 and IFI16 are NET-bound SLE autoantigens.
source: In summary, our immunostaining experiments provide evidence that AIM2 and IFI16 bind NETs in the setting of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, establishing AIM2 and IFI16 as NET-bound SLE autoantigens.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined evidence of autoantibody presence, NET binding in vitro, and NET co-localization in tissues.

claim: Systemic lupus erythematosus is characterized by upregulated interferon expression and autoantibody production.
source: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a rheumatic disease characterized by upregulated interferon (IFN) expression and autoantibody production (Gupta and Kaplan, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Gupta and Kaplan, 2021).

claim: Many SLE autoantigens are nucleic acid binding proteins.
source: Many SLE autoantigens are nucleic acid binding proteins, and nucleic acid containing immune complexes are implicated in aspects of pathogenesis (Mahajan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Mahajan et al., 2016).

claim: Nucleic acid containing immune complexes are implicated in aspects of SLE pathogenesis.
source: Many SLE autoantigens are nucleic acid binding proteins, and nucleic acid containing immune complexes are implicated in aspects of pathogenesis (Mahajan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Mahajan et al., 2016).

claim: The AIM2-like receptors are a group of IFN-induced innate sensors of double-stranded DNA.
source: The AIM2-like receptors (ALRs) are a group of IFN-induced innate sensors of double-stranded (ds) DNA.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the ALR protein family.

claim: AIM2 and IFI16 are the most studied members of the ALR family.
source: AIM2 and IFI16 are the most studied members of the ALR family, which also includes IFIX and MNDA.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the ALR protein family.

claim: The ALR family includes IFIX and MNDA in addition to AIM2 and IFI16.
source: AIM2 and IFI16 are the most studied members of the ALR family, which also includes IFIX and MNDA.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the ALR protein family.

claim: ALRs bind to dsDNA in a sequence-independent manner via electrostatic interactions with the dsDNA backbone.
source: The ALRs bind to dsDNA in a sequence-independent manner via electrostatic interactions with the dsDNA backbone and form an oligomerized filament along areas of accessible dsDNA of any origin (Morrone et al., 2014; Morrone et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Morrone et al., 2014; Morrone et al., 2015).

claim: ALRs form an oligomerized filament along areas of accessible dsDNA of any origin.
source: The ALRs bind to dsDNA in a sequence-independent manner via electrostatic interactions with the dsDNA backbone and form an oligomerized filament along areas of accessible dsDNA of any origin (Morrone et al., 2014; Morrone et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Morrone et al., 2014; Morrone et al., 2015).

claim: ALRs activate downstream innate immune signaling by type I IFN and inflammasome (IL-1/IL-18) pathways.
source: Once activated, the ALRs activate downstream innate immune signaling by type I IFN and inflammasome (IL-1/IL-18) pathways (Hornung et al., 2009; Unterholzner et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Hornung et al., 2009; Unterholzner et al., 2010).

claim: Anti-IFI16 antibodies occur in both SLE and Sjogren's Syndrome.
source: Anti-IFI16 antibodies occur in both SLE and Sjogren's Syndrome (SS), but we have previously reported that the targeted epitopes differ in these diseases (Antiochos et al., 2018; Baer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work by the authors (Antiochos et al., 2018; Baer et al., 2016).

claim: The targeted epitopes of IFI16 differ between SLE and Sjogren's Syndrome.
source: Anti-IFI16 antibodies occur in both SLE and Sjogren's Syndrome (SS), but we have previously reported that the targeted epitopes differ in these diseases (Antiochos et al., 2018; Baer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work by the authors (Antiochos et al., 2018; Baer et al., 2016).

claim: IFI16 oligomers appear to be recognized by Sjogren's Syndrome sera.
source: IFI16 oligomers appear to be recognized by SS sera, suggesting that dsDNA binding may enhance its antigenicity.
evidence: This is inferred from prior work on IFI16 antibodies in SS.

claim: dsDNA binding may enhance IFI16 antigenicity.
source: IFI16 oligomers appear to be recognized by SS sera, suggesting that dsDNA binding may enhance its antigenicity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that oligomers are recognized.

claim: AIM2 assembles similar filamentous structures on dsDNA as IFI16.
source: While AIM2 assembles similar filamentous structures on dsDNA, its status as an autoantigen has not been reported.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AIM2 structure and function.

claim: NETs are microbicidal structures consisting of protein-laden chromatin fibers generated by neutrophils in response to various stimuli.
source: NETs are microbicidal structures consisting of protein-laden chromatin fibers generated by neutrophils in response to various stimuli (Brinkmann et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Brinkmann et al., 2004).

claim: The NET dsDNA scaffold is a structure on which a variety of molecules interact.
source: The NET dsDNA scaffold is a structure on which a variety of molecules interact (Gugliesi et al., 2013), representing a platform for antigenic materials (including SLE autoantigens) to be presented to the adaptive immune system (Mistry and Kaplan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Gugliesi et al., 2013).

claim: NETs represent a platform for antigenic materials (including SLE autoantigens) to be presented to the adaptive immune system.
source: The NET dsDNA scaffold is a structure on which a variety of molecules interact (Gugliesi et al., 2013), representing a platform for antigenic materials (including SLE autoantigens) to be presented to the adaptive immune system (Mistry and Kaplan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Mistry and Kaplan, 2017).

claim: IFI16 and AIM2 nucleoprotein filaments are highly stable and persist even after the dsDNA template has been degraded by nucleases.
source: IFI16 and AIM2 nucleoprotein filaments are highly stable and persist even after the dsDNA template has been degraded by nucleases (Antiochos et al., 2018; Matyszewski et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Antiochos et al., 2018; Matyszewski et al., 2018).

claim: Impaired clearance of NETs by DNase I has been observed in some SLE patients.
source: IFI16 and AIM2 nucleoprotein filaments are highly stable and persist even after the dsDNA template has been degraded by nucleases (Antiochos et al., 2018; Matyszewski et al., 2018), and impaired clearance of NETs by DNase I has been observed in some SLE patients (Hakkim et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Hakkim et al., 2010).

claim: DNase I is the nuclease responsible for effective clearance of NETs.
source: We used DNase I to explore this question, as DNase I is the nuclease responsible for effective clearance of NETs (Hakkim et al., 2010), and DNase I deficiency has been associated with SLE in both human subjects and animal models (Martínez Valle et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Hakkim et al., 2010).

claim: DNase I deficiency has been associated with SLE in both human subjects and animal models.
source: We used DNase I to explore this question, as DNase I is the nuclease responsible for effective clearance of NETs (Hakkim et al., 2010), and DNase I deficiency has been associated with SLE in both human subjects and animal models (Martínez Valle et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Martínez Valle et al., 2008).

claim: Prior studies have presented evidence of in vivo NET formation within the renal tissues of SLE patients.
source: Prior studies have presented evidence of in vivo NET formation within the renal tissues of SLE patients, supporting the notion that dysregulated neutrophil function contributes to immune pathology in this disease (Villanueva et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Villanueva et al., 2011).

claim: Dysregulated neutrophil function contributes to immune pathology in SLE.
source: Prior studies have presented evidence of in vivo NET formation within the renal tissues of SLE patients, supporting the notion that dysregulated neutrophil function contributes to immune pathology in this disease (Villanueva et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Villanueva et al., 2011).

claim: Patients with diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis harbor netting neutrophils in renal tissue.
source: Considering that patients with diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis are known to harbor netting neutrophils in renal tissue (Villanueva et al., 2011), we identified patients with diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, then selected 5 samples whose biopsies demonstrated neutrophilic infiltrates or karyorrhectic debris (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Villanueva et al., 2011).

claim: NETosis is a process whereby dsDNA is expelled into the extracellular space at sites of tissue damage and is of mechanistic relevance in SLE.
source: NETosis is a process whereby dsDNA is expelled into the extracellular space at sites of tissue damage and is of mechanistic relevance in SLE (Gupta and Kaplan, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Gupta and Kaplan, 2016).

claim: The NET dsDNA scaffold is a source of antigenic proteins in SLE and other inflammatory diseases.
source: The NET dsDNA scaffold is a structure on which a variety of molecules can interact, and is a source of antigenic proteins in SLE and other inflammatory diseases (Mistry and Kaplan, 2017; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Mistry and Kaplan, 2017; Lee et al., 2017).

claim: IFI16 is released from epithelial cells injured by the NK cell granule killing pathway.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that IFI16 is released from epithelial cells injured by the NK cell granule killing pathway and that IFI16 retains its ability to interact with dsDNA in the extracellular space (Antiochos et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work by the authors (Antiochos et al., 2018).

claim: IFI16 retains its ability to interact with dsDNA in the extracellular space.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that IFI16 is released from epithelial cells injured by the NK cell granule killing pathway and that IFI16 retains its ability to interact with dsDNA in the extracellular space (Antiochos et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work by the authors (Antiochos et al., 2018).

claim: IFI16 is released from irradiated epithelial cells.
source: Our findings are consistent with the observations that (i) IFI16 is released from irradiated epithelial cells, and (ii) extracellular IFI16 is quantifiable in the sera of SLE patients (Gugliesi et al., 2013; Iannucci et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Gugliesi et al., 2013; Iannucci et al., 2020).

claim: Extracellular IFI16 is quantifiable in the sera of SLE patients.
source: Our findings are consistent with the observations that (i) IFI16 is released from irradiated epithelial cells, and (ii) extracellular IFI16 is quantifiable in the sera of SLE patients (Gugliesi et al., 2013; Iannucci et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Gugliesi et al., 2013; Iannucci et al., 2020).

claim: AIM2 is released from pyroptotic cells into extracellular vesicles in the context of pyroptosis.
source: In addition, the release of AIM2 from pyroptotic cells into extracellular vesicles in the context of pyroptosis has been described (So et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (So et al., 2018).

claim: Extracellular signaling activities of the related oligomerizing inflammasome adaptor protein ASC have been reported.
source: In addition, the release of AIM2 from pyroptotic cells into extracellular vesicles in the context of pyroptosis has been described (So et al., 2018) and extracellular signaling activities of the related oligomerizing inflammasome adaptor protein ASC have also been reported (Franklin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Franklin et al., 2014).

claim: NETs promote IFN signaling at sites of their generation when engulfed by immune cells.
source: NETs promote IFN signaling at sites of their generation when engulfed by immune cells (Garcia-Romo et al., 2011; Apel et al., 2021), and may have additional disease-amplifying functions (Salazar-Gonzalez et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Garcia-Romo et al., 2011; Apel et al., 2021).

claim: NETs may have additional disease-amplifying functions beyond promoting IFN signaling.
source: NETs promote IFN signaling at sites of their generation when engulfed by immune cells (Garcia-Romo et al., 2011; Apel et al., 2021), and may have additional disease-amplifying functions (Salazar-Gonzalez et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Salazar-Gonzalez et al., 2019).

claim: Extracellular ALRs may enhance IFN signaling at sites of neutrophil activation by prolonging the stability of interferogenic NETs.
source: By prolonging the stability of interferogenic NETs, extracellular ALRs may enhance IFN signaling at sites of neutrophil activation, which could be further amplified by IFN-induced expression of the ALRs themselves.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed DNase resistance of ALR-bound NETs and known IFN-inducing properties of NETs.

claim: IFN-induced expression of ALRs could further amplify IFN signaling at sites of neutrophil activation.
source: By prolonging the stability of interferogenic NETs, extracellular ALRs may enhance IFN signaling at sites of neutrophil activation, which could be further amplified by IFN-induced expression of the ALRs themselves.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about a potential positive feedback loop involving IFN and ALRs.

claim: Impairment of NET removal has been specifically linked to the presence of lupus nephritis.
source: Impairment of NET removal has been specifically linked to the presence of lupus nephritis (Hakkim et al., 2010) - a manifestation of SLE with significant associated morbidity (Gasparotto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Hakkim et al., 2010).

claim: Lupus nephritis is a manifestation of SLE with significant associated morbidity.
source: Impairment of NET removal has been specifically linked to the presence of lupus nephritis (Hakkim et al., 2010) - a manifestation of SLE with significant associated morbidity (Gasparotto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Gasparotto et al., 2020).

claim: Neutrophilic infiltration of the kidney is a feature of more severe forms of glomerulonephritis.
source: Neutrophilic infiltration of the kidney is a feature of more severe forms of glomerulonephritis, and NET formation in this organ may contribute to renal damage through the propagation of IFN signaling, immune cell activation, and thrombosis (Salazar-Gonzalez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about glomerulonephritis.
